question: What does a VDF service give the pilot?

options.text: A glide path to the runway
A bearing to or from a ground station
An automatic position on a map display
A distance from a ground station

explanation: VDF measures the direction of the aircraft's own VHF transmission at a ground station and passes the bearing back by voice. It can be used for homing, or two or more bearings can give a fix.

question: How is a VDF bearing passed to the pilot?

options.text: As a Morse identifier on the NDB frequency
By data link to the flight management system
On a dedicated VDF display in the cockpit
By voice on the VHF communication frequency

explanation: The aircraft transmits on a normal VHF voice channel (118–137 MHz, A3E) and the controller reads the bearing back by voice. The aircraft needs nothing more than its VHF radio.

question: What equipment does the aircraft need to obtain a VDF bearing?

options.text: Only a VHF communications radio
A VHF radio and an ADF receiver
A VOR receiver and a DME
A transponder and a VHF radio

explanation: All the direction-finding equipment — the special aerial array and the display — is on the ground. The aircraft just transmits on its VHF voice radio.

question: On which frequency is automatic triangulation by VDF available?

options.text: 243.0 MHz, the military distress frequency
118.0 MHz, the lowest VHF voice channel
121.5 MHz, the international distress frequency
Any VHF approach frequency of the station

explanation: Auto-triangulation, where several VDF stations combine bearings to give a position automatically, is provided only on 121.5 MHz. UHF DF is limited to military use.

question: Why is VDF rarely used for routine navigation today?

options.text: It needs a separate receiver that few aircraft carry
It is permitted only in military aircraft
It works only below 1 000 ft above the station
Much more accurate and capable systems are now available

explanation: VDF is simple and needs only a VHF radio, but VOR, DME, RNAV and GNSS are far more accurate and need no controller workload. It remains useful as a back-up and for emergencies.

question: Where are aeronautical stations offering VDF listed?

options.text: In the aerodrome (AD) section of the AIP
Only on the approach charts for each runway
In the en route (ENR) section of the NOTAMs
In the aircraft's flight manual

explanation: VDF stations are listed in the aerodrome section of the AIP. Some state that the service is not for en route navigation except in an emergency.

question: When may a VDF station decline to give a bearing?

options.text: When the aircraft is flying above FL 100
When conditions are poor or outside calibrated limits
Whenever the aircraft is more than 25 NM away
When the pilot has not filed a flight plan

explanation: Bearings are given only when conditions are satisfactory and the bearing lies within the station's calibrated limits. If it cannot be given, the pilot is told why.

question: What is a QDM?

options.text: The magnetic bearing of the aircraft from the station
The true track to the station
The magnetic heading to steer (no wind) to the station
The true bearing of the aircraft from the station

explanation: QDM is the magnetic direction TO the station (ignoring wind), used for homing and published let-downs. Its reciprocal is the QDR.

question: What is a QDR?

options.text: The relative bearing of the station from the aircraft
The magnetic bearing of the aircraft from the station
The true bearing of the aircraft from the station
The magnetic heading to steer to the station

explanation: QDR is the magnetic bearing FROM the station — effectively the radial the aircraft is on. It is used for en route navigation.

question: What is a QTE?

options.text: The magnetic heading to steer to the station
The true track from the aircraft to the station
The magnetic bearing of the aircraft from the station
The true bearing of the aircraft from the station

explanation: QTE is the true bearing FROM the station, used for en route position lines. Its reciprocal, the true direction TO the station, is the QUJ.

question: What is a QUJ?

options.text: The true track to the station
The true bearing from the station
The magnetic bearing from the station
The magnetic track to the station

explanation: QUJ is the true direction TO the station. It is the reciprocal of QTE and is not generally used.

question: Which pair of Q codes are reciprocals of each other?

options.text: QDM and QUJ
QDM and QTE
QDM and QDR
QDR and QTE

explanation: QDM (magnetic to) and QDR (magnetic from) differ by 180°; so do QUJ (true to) and QTE (true from). QDM and QTE, for example, differ by 180° plus the variation.

question: An aircraft is given a QDR of 070°. What is its QDM?
explanation: QDM is the reciprocal of QDR: 070° + 180° = 250°. Both are magnetic, so variation does not enter into it.

question: A station reports a QTE of 120°. Variation at the station is 5°W. What is the QDM?
explanation: Magnetic = true + west variation: QDR = 120° + 5° = 125°. QDM is its reciprocal: 125° + 180° = 305°. Applying the variation the wrong way gives 295°.

question: A station gives a true bearing from the station of 353°. Variation is 8°E. What is the QDR?
explanation: Magnetic = true − east variation: 353° − 8° = 345°. The QDM would be 165° and the QUJ 173°.

question: A pilot requests a QDM and is given 040°. Which way is the station from the aircraft?

options.text: 40° to the right of the aircraft's nose
On a true bearing of 040° from the aircraft
On a magnetic bearing of 040° from the aircraft
On a magnetic bearing of 220° from the aircraft

explanation: A QDM is the magnetic direction to the station: in still air, steering 040°M takes the aircraft to it. The aircraft itself is on the 220° QDR.

question: What accuracy does a Class A VDF bearing have?

options.text: Within ±10°
Within ±2°
Within ±0.5°
Within ±5°

explanation: Class A ±2°, Class B ±5°, Class C ±10°, Class D worse than Class C.

question: What accuracy does a Class B VDF bearing have?

options.text: Within ±5°
Within ±2°
Within ±10°
Within ±1°

explanation: Class B bearings are accurate to ±5°. Normally nothing better than Class B is offered.

question: What accuracy does a Class C VDF bearing have?

options.text: Within ±5°
Worse than ±10°
Within ±10°
Within ±2°

explanation: Class C is ±10°. Class D is anything less accurate than Class C.

question: A VDF bearing is passed with no class stated. What accuracy can normally be assumed?

options.text: ±10°, Class C
±0.5°, Doppler accuracy
±2°, Class A
±5°, Class B

explanation: Bearings better than Class B are not normally available, so unless told otherwise the pilot should assume ±5°.

question: What accuracy can modern Doppler VDF equipment achieve?

options.text: About ±2°
About ±5°
About ±10°
About ±0.5°

explanation: The latest equipment uses the Doppler principle to produce a high-resolution digital bearing, accurate to about ±0.5° on VHF and UHF.

question: In what order does a VDF station reply to a bearing request?

options.text: The bearing, the time, the Q code, then the class
Q code, bearing, class, then time if asked
The time, the bearing, the class, then the Q code
Class, Q code, bearing, then the time of the observation

explanation: The reply gives the appropriate phrase or Q code, the bearing in degrees, the class of bearing, and the time of observation if asked for.

question: Why is the VDF ground aerial array made of vertical elements?

options.text: Aircraft VHF voice transmissions are vertically polarized
Vertical elements reject sky-wave interference at night
Vertical elements are needed to receive UHF only
Horizontal elements would give a 180° ambiguity

explanation: VHF communications aerials radiate vertically polarized signals, so the receiving array uses vertical elements arranged in a circle. Bearings can be displayed relative to true or magnetic north at the station.

question: What decides the range of a VDF station?

options.text: Only the time of day and the season
Only the power of the ground transmitter
Line of sight, terrain, power and the atmosphere
Surface wave attenuation over the land and the sea between

explanation: VDF uses VHF, so range follows the line-of-sight formula and is limited by high ground. Transmitter power also limits it, and temperature and humidity gradients can give more than line-of-sight range.

question: An aircraft at 6 400 ft calls a VDF station whose aerial is at 400 ft. What is the maximum theoretical range?

options.text: 98 NM
123 NM
80 NM
101 NM

explanation: 1.23 × (√6 400 + √400) = 1.23 × (80 + 20) = 1.23 × 100 = 123 NM. Ignoring the station height gives about 98 NM; adding the heights under one root gives about 101 NM.

question: A VDF station 200 NM away has its aerial at 2 500 ft. What is the lowest altitude at which the aircraft can expect contact?

options.text: About 600 ft
About 2 500 ft
About 12 700 ft
About 26 400 ft

explanation: 200 / 1.23 ≈ 162.6 = √h + √2 500 = √h + 50, so √h ≈ 112.6 and h ≈ 12 700 ft. Forgetting to subtract the station's own 50 gives about 26 400 ft.

question: What is site error in VDF?

options.text: Errors from the aircraft banking while transmitting
Errors from two aircraft transmitting at the same time
Errors from the bearing being read in true instead of in magnetic
Reflections from buildings or terrain at the site

explanation: Reflections from buildings at the site, and from terrain on the way to it (propagation error), distort the direction of the arriving signal.

question: Why are VDF bearings most accurate when the aircraft flies straight and level?

options.text: The aerials are vertically polarized; bank upsets this
Turning causes coastal refraction of the VHF signal
The ground station can only track aircraft at constant heading
The VHF radio transmits only when the wings are level

explanation: Banking tilts the aircraft's vertical aerial, changing the polarization of the transmitted signal and degrading the bearing.

question: Why is VDF accuracy poor when the aircraft is overhead the station?

options.text: The line-of-sight range is zero directly overhead
Direct and reflected waves cause fading and errors
The aircraft is in the station's sky-wave dead space there
The bearing changes from true to magnetic overhead

explanation: Close overhead, direct and reflected waves (and other multipath) can cause brief fading or loss and large bearing errors — especially with the newer Doppler equipment.

question: What effect do two aircraft transmitting at the same time have on VDF?

options.text: Momentary bearing errors
A permanent loss of the VDF service
An increase in range for both aircraft
An automatic change to Class A bearings

explanation: Synchronous transmissions confuse the direction finder and give brief errors in the bearing.

question: For what purposes can VDF bearings be used?

options.text: Automatic landings and runway centre line guidance
Collision avoidance, altitude reporting and homing
Track checks, position lines, homing and let-downs
Distance checks, glide path guidance and taxiing

explanation: VDF gives bearings only, which serve as track checks, position lines for a fix, homing to the station and published VDF let-down procedures.
